content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has been actively involved in addressing issues related to maternal, child, and adolescent health (MCA), as well as mental health and substance abuse (MSD). Key members of the WHO secretariat include Rajiv Bahl, Anthony Costello, Tarun Dua, Nigel Rollins, and Shekhar Saxena from WHO Geneva, along with Pablo Duran from the Centro Latinoamericano de Perinatología and Pilar Ramón-Pardo from the WHO Regional Office for the Americas. Additional support was provided by staff from the WHO Incident Management System in Geneva, including Ian Clarke, Margaret Harris, Anaïs Legand, and William Perea. The development of guidelines for the screening, assessment, and management of neonates and infants exposed to the Zika virus in utero involved contributions from various experts. Dr. Ganeshwaran H. Mochida and Dr. Archana A. Patel, both affiliated with Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, were engaged as consultants to review evidence and draft the guidelines. Dylan J. Vaughan assisted with literature retrieval, while Michelle Griffin and Steven Morris from Public Health England supported the preparation and documentation of the guideline meetings. The guideline development group included a diverse team of international experts: Satinder Aneja (Lady Hardinge Medical College, India), James Barkovich (University of California, San Francisco, USA), Marianne Besnard (Ta’aone Hospital, Tahiti), J. Helen Cross (Institute of Child Health, London, UK), Richard Leventer (Royal Children’s Hospital, University of Melbourne, Australia), Amira Masri (University of Jordan, Jordan), Cynthia Moore (CDC, USA), Charles Newton (Kenya Medical Research Institute, Kenya), Alessandra Barroso Penna e Costa (Fernandes Figueira Institute, Brazil), Tania Saad Salles (Ministry of Health, Brazil), Vanessa van der Linden (Recife, Brazil), and Khalid Yunis (American University of Beirut, Lebanon). The recommendations were developed under WHO emergency procedures and were valid until December 2016. Routine literature reviews were planned to assess the need for updates, particularly concerning the spectrum of diseases associated with Zika virus exposure. The WHO departments of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health, along with Mental Health and Substance Abuse, were tasked with reviewing and updating the guidance as necessary. WHO also welcomed feedback and suggestions regarding the content of the guidelines. The references cited in the document include key studies and reports on the Zika virus, its association with microcephaly, and congenital Zika syndrome. These references span a wide range of topics, including epidemiological studies, clinical findings, neuroimaging, and public health responses. The cited works provide a comprehensive foundation for understanding the impact of Zika virus infection on maternal and child health, as well as the broader implications for public health and clinical management.
